keyframe_review.note: 523-660, 507.8 km2. The page dates the founding to 534 ('Wihtgar and Stuf received the island from Cerdic's son Cynric in 534, with the death of Wihtgar taking place in 544') and says Wihtgar 'may be fictitious, a founding myth invented to explain the island's name'; Cliopatria starts in 523, for which the page has no support. The outline is the island, unchanged, from 534. Infobox: the island is '147-square-mile (380 km2)'; Cliopatria's 507.8 km2 is 1.34 times that (within the factor of two; the shape includes the surrounding coastal cells, and the gazetteer's Isle of Wight resolves to 506 km2).

ledger.note: 534: Wihtgar and Stuf receive the Isle of Wight from Cynric. 'Wihtgar and Stuf received the island from Cerdic's son Cynric in 534, with the death of Wihtgar taking place in 544'; Asser calls them nephews of Cerdic, of Jutish and Gothic origin, who set out to exterminate the native Britons; scholars suggest Wihtgar may be fictitious.

region.text: the Isle of Wight, 'the Early Medieval inhabitants of the Isle of Wight'

ledger.note: 661: Wulfhere of Mercia conquers the Isle of Wight and gives it to Sussex. 'Wulfhere of Mercia conquered the island in 661 and gave overlordship to his godson, King Æthelwealh of Sussex', to convert the islanders. The Wulfhere page agrees: 'Wulfhere raided the Isle of Wight in 661. He then gave the island and the Meonware (the Meon valley) to his godson, King Æthelwealh of the South Saxons.' The vassal's record: the counterpart is the overlord; Sussex's dossier carries the mirror.

region.text: the Isle of Wight, 'the Early Medieval inhabitants of the Isle of Wight'

ledger.note: 686: Cædwalla of Wessex invades the Isle of Wight. Bede: 'the island was converted after an invasion in 686 by King Cædwalla of Wessex'; the Chronicle has the invasion made with Cædwalla's brother Mul of Kent. Arwald, the 'last heathen Anglo-Saxon king', was 'purportedly killed while resisting Cædwalla'.

region.text: the Isle of Wight, 'the Early Medieval inhabitants of the Isle of Wight'

ledger.note: 686: the island passes to Wessex. 'After this point, the island became a part of Wessex and later England.' Bede has Arwald's two younger brothers captured, baptised and executed on Cædwalla's orders (the Cædwalla page adds that they were found at Stoneham in Hampshire).

wars.outcome: Arwald, the last heathen Anglo-Saxon king, died resisting; his brothers were executed; the island became part of Wessex.
wars.note: Mul of Kent took part per the Chronicle. The Cædwalla page gives no year for the conquest and says Cædwalla vowed a quarter of the island to the church; the Wihtwara page's 686 is used.

certainty.note: The island's shore is a natural limit; no page opened gives a treaty or survey line, and the kingdom's existence in the early centuries is partly legendary.

notes: Cliopatria's Wihtgar row (523..691) is trimmed to 534..686 on the Wihtwara page and bridged across the 661-665 gap. The page treats Wihtgar as possibly fictitious and the Jutish settlement as undated; the 530 Chronicle entry and the burial at Wihtgaresbyrig are not on the page opened. The kingdom is recorded as independent from 534, with the status after 544 and before 661 unrecorded ('formed an independent kingdom at points'). The Sussex dossier carries the mirror vassal pair (661, 686) and the Wessex dossier the 686 gain. Capital: none named on the pages opened, a placeholder dot is used. Three pages were opened (the Wihtwara, Cædwalla and Wulfhere articles, the last two shared with the Sussex dossier), a little over the 1-2 page budget.
